newsitem.title: UK: Gold above lows, dollar slips,stocks revive.
newsitem.headline: Gold above lows, dollar slips,stocks revive.

text.p: Gold slid to new 12-year lows on Monday as investors took flight, fearing that central banks could offload more of their official gold reserves.
On currency markets, the dollar lost ground with news of a rising Japanese trade surplus boosting the yen and renewed jitters on European economic and monetary union (EMU) helping the mark.
The Frankfurt stock market hit another record high, topping 4,000 points on the 30-share DAX index for the first time in after-hours electronic trading as Wall Street also scaled new heights.
Paris shares made more moderate gains, while the London stock market ended marginally lower, erasing most of an earlier fall prompted by fears of higher interest rates.
The Dow Jones industrial average of U.S. blue chip stocks was up around a third of a percent as European markets closed.
Gold dropped to a low of $314.10, down more than $10 from Friday, before recovering to end London trading around $318.55 as speculators cashed in their profits.
"There is some support at $315 but it's hard to tell how much -- we haven't seen these levels for 12 years," one London-based bullion dealer said.
"It would take a Martian to be bullish at this point," said Andy Smith, analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland. "Expect an orgy of selling over the next few weeks," another bullion dealer added.
Gold plunged to 12-year lows last week after the Reserve Bank of Australia said it had sold 167 tonnes from its gold reserves.

Following earlier disposals by the Belgian and Dutch central banks, this pushed already nervous investors to sell for fear that more central banks would get rid of some of the 35,000 tonnes of gold they own.
Gold has now lost around $50 since January, putting the future of some mines in doubt.

The yen was boosted to four-week highs around 112 to the dollar after news of a 129.3-percent year-on-year gain in Japan's trade surplus for the first 20 days of June. The dollar also suffered from receding hopes for higher U.S. interest rates in the near term, analysts said.
"Yen strength started the move and we feel the dollar/yen pullback has further to go," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He added that the yen could benefit, too, from dollar sales by south east Asian central banks seeking to avoid contagion from Thailand's currency crisis.
The dollar also came under pressure from the mark as the pound dipped on weak industrial output data and suffered further from market nerves over Europe's progress towards EMU.
As some German politicians continue to speak out for a delay in EMU, the mark has gained favour in the short term.

In an interview in the Financial Times, Bavarian prime minister Edmund Stoiber, a member of the Christian Social Union party of Theo Waigel, Germany's finance minister, said an EMU delay would be preferable to a weak single currency.
Currency dealers said that although the market still expected EMU to start on time in 1999, calls for a delay have raised some doubts.

"You can argue there will be safe-haven buying of marks because the soft euro is questioned, or that investors will want to get out of Euorope altogether and into dollars, sterling or maybe Swiss francs," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, meanwhile, said the Group of 10 top industrial nations would continue to monitor currency markets closely but avoided comment on recent dollar strength.
In equity markets, German shares advanced to more records, boosted by a revival of the dollar from its lows -- better news for exporters -- and Wall Street's lead.
"The risk in the German share market at the moment is not to be invested in it," Susanne Schneemayer at Hypo-Research said in a market commentary.

After early gains, the London stock market was dragged down by a fall in futures amid speculation that the newly-independent Bank of England would raise interest rates this week to keep the economy from overheating.

But Wall Street later came to its rescue and trading was also buoyed by a successful debut by the latest building society-turned-bank to float on the stock market, Woolwich. Woolwich topped its tipped debut level of around 320 pence at a closing 333 but was well below a high of 370.
The Paris bourse closed higher after a weaker start as gains on Wall Street outweighed a weaker dollar.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was around 112.30 yen and 1.7458 marks, compared with 113.74 and 1.7565 in late European business on Friday. Sterling was around 2.9490 marks versus 2.9597.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 2.1 points or 0.04 percent at 4,810.7 but was well above its 4,776.4 low.

FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended bourse floor trade up 30.31 points or 0.77 percent at a record close of 3,972.84. In later electronic trade the IBIS DAX index was up 56.62 points or 1.43 percent at 4,003.35.
PARIS - The CAC-40 finished 13.18 points or 0.45 percent higher at 2,947.66.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended London trading around $318.55 an ounce, up from its lows but well down from Friday's late $324.50. Silver declined 10 cents to $4.45.
